input: The town council of Eastbrook voted on Monday to convert the old railway depot into a public library and community workshop. The building has been empty since the line closed in 2009. Renovation will cost an estimated 4.2 million euros, two thirds of which will come from a regional heritage fund. Construction is scheduled to begin next spring and take about eighteen months. Residents had campaigned for the project for years, arguing that the town's current library is too small and has no space for events. The new site will include a reading room, a makerspace with 3D printers and a café run by a local social enterprise.
expected: Eastbrook's council approved turning the disused railway depot into a library and community workshop, a 4.2 million euro project largely funded by a heritage fund that starts next spring.

input: A study of 1,200 office workers found that people who took a ten-minute walk after lunch reported feeling less tired in the afternoon than those who stayed at their desks. The researchers asked participants to rate their energy levels every hour for four weeks. Walkers also completed slightly more tasks, although the difference in productivity was small and not statistically significant. The authors caution that participants chose whether to walk, so more energetic people may simply have been more likely to take a walk in the first place. They are now planning a randomized trial.
expected: In a four-week study of 1,200 office workers, those who walked for ten minutes after lunch felt less tired in the afternoon, but the effect on productivity was small and the authors plan a randomized trial to rule out self-selection.

input: The city's bike-sharing scheme recorded its busiest year ever, with 3.1 million rides, up 40 percent from the previous year. Officials credit the addition of 800 electric bikes and 60 new docking stations in outer neighbourhoods. The average ride lasted 14 minutes. However, the operator warned that vandalism and theft cost it nearly half a million euros, and that some stations in the centre are often empty during the morning rush. The city plans to use trucks to redistribute bikes more often and is testing a discount for riders who return bikes to understocked stations.
expected: Bike-share rides rose 40 percent to a record 3.1 million thanks to new e-bikes and stations, though vandalism costs and empty central stations remain problems the city plans to tackle with redistribution and incentives.

input: After three years of testing, a small bakery in the harbour district has switched all of its ovens from gas to electricity powered by rooftop solar panels and a battery. The owner says energy costs have fallen by about a third, although the upfront investment of 90,000 euros will take roughly seven years to pay back. The bakery had to adjust several recipes because the electric ovens heat more evenly, which changed the crust on its signature rye bread. Regular customers were invited to blind tastings to help fine-tune the new baking times.
expected: A harbour-district bakery moved from gas to solar-powered electric ovens, cutting energy costs by a third with a seven-year payback, and adjusted recipes with help from customer tastings.

input: The national weather service has issued an amber warning for heavy snow across the northern hills from Thursday evening until Saturday morning. Up to 30 centimetres may fall on higher ground, with strong winds causing drifts. Travel disruption is likely, and some rural communities could be cut off for a time. Schools will decide on closures on Friday morning. The service advises drivers to avoid unnecessary journeys and to carry blankets, water and a charged phone if they must travel.
expected: An amber warning for up to 30 cm of snow and drifting in the northern hills from Thursday evening to Saturday morning means likely travel disruption, and drivers are urged to avoid unnecessary journeys.

input: Volunteers counted 212 species of birds during this year's weekend census at the lake reserve, the highest number since counts began in 1995. Highlights included a pair of breeding ospreys, which had not nested at the lake for over a century. Experts attribute the increase to the restoration of reed beds and the removal of invasive fish that competed with birds for food. Not all the news was good: numbers of swifts and house martins continued to decline, reflecting a national trend linked to fewer insects.
expected: The lake reserve's bird census found a record 212 species, including nesting ospreys for the first time in a century thanks to habitat restoration, while swifts and house martins kept declining.

input: A software company has announced that all employees can work a four-day week without a pay cut, following a six-month pilot. During the pilot, the number of support tickets resolved per week stayed the same and staff turnover fell. Managers reported that meetings became shorter and more focused. Customers will still be able to reach support five days a week because teams will stagger their days off. The company says it will review the policy every year and may reverse it if key targets are missed.
expected: After a successful six-month pilot with stable output and lower turnover, a software company is giving all staff a four-day week at full pay, with staggered days off and an annual review.

input: The museum's new exhibition brings together 70 maps drawn between the 15th and 19th centuries, many shown in public for the first time. Visitors can see how coastlines, trade routes and even imaginary islands appeared and disappeared as explorers returned with new information. A digital table lets visitors overlay historic maps on modern satellite images. The curators hope the exhibition will show that maps were never neutral: they reflected the interests of the people who paid for them. The exhibition runs until the end of March and entry is free for under-18s.
expected: A new museum exhibition of 70 historic maps, many never shown before, explores how maps changed with exploration and reflected their sponsors' interests; it runs until March and is free for under-18s.

input: The regional hospital has opened a night clinic for minor injuries to reduce waiting times in its emergency department. The clinic is staffed by nurse practitioners and is open from 6 pm to midnight. In its first month it treated 1,900 patients, mostly with sprains, cuts and minor burns. Average waiting times in the emergency department dropped from four hours to just under three. Hospital managers want to extend the clinic's hours but say they first need to recruit more staff.
expected: The regional hospital's new evening minor-injuries clinic treated 1,900 patients in its first month and cut emergency waiting times from four hours to under three; longer hours depend on recruiting staff.

input: Researchers have developed a low-cost sensor that detects when bread starts to go stale by measuring changes in moisture and the gases it releases. The sensor, about the size of a coin, could be placed inside packaging and linked to a phone app. Supermarkets testing the device hope to reduce waste by discounting products at the right moment instead of throwing them away. The team says the sensor costs less than five cents to produce, but it still needs approval for contact with food before it can be used widely.
expected: A coin-sized sensor costing under five cents can detect stale bread from moisture and gas changes, helping supermarkets cut waste, but it still needs food-contact approval.

input: Local farmers have formed a cooperative to sell vegetables directly to schools in the district. Instead of relying on wholesalers, the cooperative delivers seasonal produce twice a week, and school cooks plan menus around what is available. Parents say children are eating more vegetables, partly because classes visit the farms to learn how the food is grown. The arrangement costs the schools about the same as before, while farmers earn more per kilo because there is no middleman.
expected: A farmers' cooperative now supplies district schools directly with seasonal vegetables, at similar cost to schools and better prices for farmers, and children are eating more vegetables.

input: The river ferry, which has carried passengers between the two villages since 1932, will be replaced by an electric vessel next summer. The new ferry can carry twelve cars instead of eight and will charge at each landing during the few minutes it takes to load. Operators expect to save 150,000 litres of diesel a year. The old ferry will not be scrapped: a heritage group plans to restore it and use it for summer excursions.
expected: Next summer an electric ferry carrying twelve cars will replace the 1932 diesel river ferry, saving 150,000 litres of fuel a year, while the old boat will be restored for excursions.

input: The Millbrook district council has approved a plan to replace all 6,400 of its street lights with LED fittings over the next three years. The project will cost 3.8 million euros, but officials expect it to cut the council's street-lighting electricity bill by about 60 percent, saving roughly 410,000 euros a year. The new lamps can also be dimmed remotely between midnight and 5 am on quiet residential roads. Some residents raised concerns at the meeting that dimmer streets could feel less safe, and one councillor asked for an independent study of night-time accidents. The council agreed to review the dimming policy after the first year.
expected: Millbrook council will spend 3.8 million euros converting 6,400 street lights to LEDs over three years, expecting to cut lighting electricity costs by about 60 percent, though night-time dimming will be reviewed after safety concerns.

input: Researchers at the Halvern Institute of Marine Biology have published the results of a two-year experiment testing whether playing recorded reef sounds can attract young fish to damaged coral. The team placed underwater speakers on 24 degraded patches of reef and left another 24 silent. Patches with speakers had on average 14 percent more juvenile fish by the end of the study, a figure that attracted wide attention online. However, the authors stress that the difference was not statistically significant, because fish numbers varied hugely from patch to patch and between seasons. They also found no difference in coral regrowth. A larger trial with 120 sites is planned for next year.
expected: A two-year Halvern Institute trial found 14 percent more juvenile fish on damaged reef patches where reef sounds were played, but the difference was not statistically significant and coral regrowth was unchanged; a 120-site trial follows.

input: The Corrin Valley health board has started offering free blood pressure checks in 18 pharmacies as part of a year-long pilot. Anyone over 40 can walk in without an appointment, and readings are shared with the patient's family doctor if they agree. In the first ten weeks, pharmacists carried out 5,300 checks and referred 640 people whose readings were high enough to need follow-up. Around a quarter of those referred said they had not seen a doctor in more than three years. Pharmacy owners welcomed the scheme but said the fee of eight euros per check barely covers staff time, and some have limited the service to quieter hours.
expected: A Corrin Valley pilot offering free walk-in blood pressure checks in 18 pharmacies carried out 5,300 checks and referred 640 people in ten weeks, but pharmacists say the eight-euro fee barely covers staff time.

input: Tessaly Outdoor, a family-owned maker of hiking boots based in Grenholm, has reported record annual sales of 46 million euros, up 18 percent on the previous year. The company says most of the growth came from its repair service, which resoles worn boots for a fixed price and now handles about 30,000 pairs a year. Online orders made up 41 percent of sales, compared with 29 percent two years ago. Profits rose more slowly, by 6 percent, because leather and shipping costs increased. The chief executive, Marta Ilves, said the firm would open a second workshop next year but had no plans to move production abroad.
expected: Boot maker Tessaly Outdoor's sales rose 18 percent to a record 46 million euros, driven largely by its repair service, though higher leather and shipping costs held profit growth to 6 percent.

input: For more than a decade, the weekly market in Pell Square has been a source of argument in Ashford Vale. Shopkeepers on the square have long complained that stalls block their entrances, while stallholders say the market brings in visitors who would not otherwise come to the town centre. A consultation last year drew 2,100 responses, roughly split between the two sides. On Tuesday, the town council finally decided to move the market to the riverside car park from April, where there is room for 60 stalls instead of 42. The council will lose about 35,000 euros a year in parking fees as a result. Stallholders' association chair Dev Okafor called the move a fair compromise.
expected: After years of dispute, Ashford Vale council voted to move the Pell Square weekly market to the riverside car park from April, making room for 60 stalls instead of 42 but costing about 35,000 euros a year in parking fees.

input: Regional rail operator Northline will add 14 extra trains a day between Carrow and Danesfield from December, the biggest timetable change on the route in twenty years. Trains will run every 20 minutes during peak hours instead of every half hour. The change follows the completion of a 9-kilometre second track near Wenlow, which removed a single-line bottleneck. Passenger numbers on the route have grown by 25 percent since 2021, and rush-hour trains are often standing room only. However, the operator admits it is still short of 11 drivers and warned that some of the new services may be cancelled at short notice until recruitment is complete.
expected: Northline will run 14 more daily trains between Carrow and Danesfield from December, with 20-minute peak frequency made possible by a new second track, but a shortage of 11 drivers may cause short-notice cancellations.

input: Heavy rain over the weekend caused the River Sorn to burst its banks in three places, flooding about 120 homes in the lower part of Kilbrae. Rainfall gauges recorded 94 millimetres in 36 hours, more than the area normally receives in a month. Emergency services evacuated 230 residents to a school sports hall, and no injuries were reported. The temporary flood barriers installed after the 2019 floods held along most of the river but were overtopped near the old mill. The regional environment agency has promised a review of the barrier height, while residents are calling for the permanent defences that were proposed five years ago and never funded.
expected: The River Sorn flooded about 120 Kilbrae homes after 94 mm of rain in 36 hours, forcing 230 evacuations; barriers were overtopped near the old mill, and residents want the permanent defences proposed five years ago.

input: A new report on emergency ambulance response times in the Brenmoor region has produced two very different readings. The regional ambulance service says the average time to reach the most urgent calls fell from nine minutes to just under eight over the past year, thanks to 12 new rapid-response cars. But the paramedics' union points out that the average hides a growing gap between town and country: in rural districts, one in five urgent calls took more than 20 minutes, up from one in eight. The union argues that the new cars were mostly based in towns. The service says rural stations will receive four cars next spring.
expected: Brenmoor's ambulance service says average response to urgent calls fell from nine to under eight minutes, but the union says rural delays worsened, with one in five urgent calls taking over 20 minutes; four rural cars arrive next spring.

input: Harrowgate Rovers have been promoted to the second division for the first time in the club's 87-year history after a 2-1 win over Lindell Athletic on Saturday. Striker Joel Amberg scored both goals, taking his total for the season to 24. The club, which only turned fully professional four years ago, finished the league seven points clear of its nearest rival. Promotion is expected to bring an extra 3 million euros in broadcasting income, but the club's stadium holds only 6,500 spectators and will need new floodlights and seating to meet second-division rules. The club has applied for a one-season exemption while the work is carried out.
expected: Harrowgate Rovers won promotion to the second division for the first time in 87 years, which is expected to bring about 3 million euros in extra broadcasting income, but their 6,500-capacity stadium needs upgrades and they have sought a one-season exemption.

input: The Ravel Street Theatre in Oskar Bay will reopen next month after a two-year restoration costing 7.5 million euros. Workers repaired the original painted ceiling, replaced 480 seats and installed a lift so that wheelchair users can reach the balcony for the first time. The theatre, built in 1908, closed in 2022 after inspectors found damage to the roof. Its first production will be a new play by local writer Hanne Sol, and tickets for the opening week sold out within two hours. The theatre's director said the building still needs a new stage machinery system, which will be installed in phases over the next three summers.
expected: Oskar Bay's 1908 Ravel Street Theatre reopens next month after a 7.5 million euro restoration that added wheelchair access to the balcony; opening week sold out, though new stage machinery will take three more summers.

input: Primary schools in the Weller district will offer free breakfast to all pupils from January, after a pilot in six schools reported better attendance. During the pilot, which ran for one school year, absence fell from 6.1 percent to 4.8 percent, while it stayed roughly flat in comparable schools. Teachers also said pupils were calmer in the first lesson of the day. Extending the scheme to all 31 primary schools will cost about 900,000 euros a year, funded from the district's education budget. Some head teachers have warned that staff will need to arrive earlier and have asked for extra pay or volunteers to supervise the breakfast clubs.
expected: All 31 Weller district primary schools will offer free breakfast from January after a pilot cut absence from 6.1 to 4.8 percent; the scheme costs about 900,000 euros a year and heads want help with supervision.

input: Shares in Brightwater Foods, a supplier of ready meals to supermarkets in the Calden region, rose 12 percent on Wednesday after the company announced a deal to supply 400 stores in the neighbouring province. Analysts estimated the contract could be worth up to 30 million euros a year, roughly a fifth of current sales. The company's chief executive described it as the most important agreement in its history. On Thursday morning, however, Brightwater issued a correction: the deal is only a letter of intent, not a signed contract, and the retailer has not committed to any volumes. The shares gave back most of their gains by the close.
expected: Brightwater Foods shares jumped 12 percent on a reported 400-store supply deal worth up to 30 million euros a year, then fell back after the company clarified it was only a letter of intent with no committed volumes.

input: The city of Varnholt has launched a free app that tells residents when their household rubbish and recycling will be collected and sends reminders the evening before. Within its first month, the app was downloaded 22,000 times, about one in five households. The city's waste department says the number of missed bin complaints fell by 30 percent over the same period, as residents put their bins out on the right day. The app was built by a team of four council developers for around 60,000 euros. Privacy campaigners have questioned why it asks for a precise location, and the council has promised to make that permission optional in the next update.
expected: Varnholt's free bin-collection reminder app reached 22,000 downloads in its first month as missed-bin complaints fell 30 percent, though after privacy concerns the precise location permission will become optional.

input: The housing association Greenfold Homes has finished building 84 affordable flats on the site of a former bus garage in Tallow End. The flats will be let at rents about 35 percent below the local market rate, with priority for key workers and families on the council waiting list. Each building has heat pumps and solar panels, which the association says will keep energy bills at roughly half the local average. More than 1,100 households applied for the first homes. The local council says the waiting list still contains 4,700 households, and campaigners say at least ten similar projects would be needed to make a real difference.
expected: Greenfold Homes has completed 84 energy-efficient affordable flats in Tallow End at rents 35 percent below market, drawing over 1,100 applications, but 4,700 households remain on the council waiting list.

input: Commuters in Pemberly have long complained about the junction where the ring road meets Stanmore Avenue, which handles about 48,000 vehicles a day. Over the past decade, traffic engineers have tried new signal timings, an extra turning lane and a ban on lorries at peak hours. Each change brought only short-lived improvements. The regional roads authority has now confirmed that it will replace the junction with a roundabout and a pedestrian underpass, at a cost of 11 million euros. Work will begin in March and take about 14 months, during which drivers should expect lane closures. Local businesses have asked for weekend-only work to limit disruption.
expected: The regional roads authority will replace Pemberly's congested Stanmore Avenue ring road junction, used by 48,000 vehicles a day, with a roundabout and underpass costing 11 million euros, with 14 months of works from March.

input: Apple growers in the Fennick Valley expect this year's harvest to be about 20 percent smaller than average after a late frost in April damaged blossoms. The growers' cooperative estimates the crop at around 38,000 tonnes, compared with a five-year average of 47,000. Orchards on lower slopes, where cold air settles, were hit hardest. Prices paid to farmers have risen by about 15 percent, which will offset some of the losses but not all. Several growers have applied for emergency loans from the regional agriculture fund. The cooperative is also testing frost-protection fans in two orchards and will report on the results next winter.
expected: A late April frost has cut the Fennick Valley apple harvest to about 38,000 tonnes, some 20 percent below average; prices up 15 percent only partly offset losses, and several growers are seeking emergency loans.

input: A community-owned wind farm near the village of Holm Ridge has completed its first full year of operation, generating 31 gigawatt hours of electricity, enough for about 8,500 homes. The five turbines were funded by 1,400 local shareholders, who will receive a return of 5.2 percent this year. A further 120,000 euros has gone into a community fund that has paid for insulation in the village hall and a minibus for elderly residents. Output was slightly below the 33 gigawatt hours forecast because of an unusually calm summer. Two neighbouring villages have now asked the cooperative to help them develop similar projects.
expected: Holm Ridge's community-owned wind farm produced 31 GWh in its first year, slightly under forecast after a calm summer, paying its 1,400 local shareholders 5.2 percent and putting 120,000 euros into a community fund.

input: A consumer group in the Leander region has found that 23 of 50 popular children's toys sold online failed basic safety tests. The group bought the toys from online marketplaces and sent them to an independent laboratory. Problems included small parts that could be swallowed, loose batteries and, in four cases, levels of a banned chemical up to 40 times the legal limit. Toys bought from established high-street shops all passed. The group has passed its findings to the regional trading standards office and is calling for online marketplaces to be made legally responsible for unsafe products sold by third-party sellers.
expected: A Leander consumer group found that 23 of 50 children's toys bought from online marketplaces failed safety tests, some containing a banned chemical at up to 40 times the limit, and wants marketplaces held legally responsible.

input: Wildlife officials in the Marren Hills reported last month that the population of the rare mountain hare had fallen by almost half since 2020, prompting calls for an emergency hunting ban. The figure was based on spring counts, which found 410 hares compared with 790 four years earlier. This week, however, the officials said the drop had been overstated. A review found that this year's count covered only 60 percent of the usual survey area because snow blocked access to several high valleys. Adjusted for the missing areas, the estimated decline is closer to 15 percent. Officials say a full recount will take place in the autumn.
expected: Marren Hills officials have corrected a reported near-halving of mountain hare numbers, saying snow limited this year's count to 60 percent of the survey area and the adjusted decline is about 15 percent; an autumn recount is planned.

input: The Kestrel Bay half marathon drew a record 9,200 runners on Sunday, more than double the number who took part five years ago. Organisers said a new flat course along the seafront helped attract first-time runners, who made up about 40 percent of the field. The men's race was won by Tomas Reval in 1 hour 3 minutes, and the women's by Ines Daru in 1 hour 11 minutes, a course record. Local cafes and hotels reported their busiest weekend of the year. However, some residents complained that road closures lasted until mid-afternoon, and the council has asked organisers to shorten them next year.
expected: A record 9,200 runners, about 40 percent of them first-timers, ran the Kestrel Bay half marathon on a new seafront course, but after complaints about long road closures the council has asked organisers to shorten them next year.

input: The Dunmore Folk Festival has announced that it will cap ticket sales at 12,000 a day next summer, down from 15,000, after this year's event was criticised for overcrowding. Visitors complained of queues of up to an hour for food stalls and toilets, and the local ambulance service treated 46 people for heat exhaustion during the three-day event. Organisers say they will also add a second entrance and double the number of free water points. The reduced capacity means ticket prices will rise by about 8 percent. Some regular visitors have welcomed the changes, while local businesses worry about fewer customers.
expected: After overcrowding complaints and 46 heat-exhaustion cases, the Dunmore Folk Festival will cut daily capacity from 15,000 to 12,000 and add an entrance and water points, though tickets will cost about 8 percent more.

input: The University of Arnsby will cut the price of student rooms in its oldest halls by 15 percent from September after a survey found that a third of first-year students were struggling to pay rent. The reduction applies to 1,300 rooms and will cost the university about 1.6 million euros a year. The university also plans to build 500 new rooms by 2028, half of which will be offered at the lower rate. The student union welcomed the move but noted that rents in newer halls, which house most international students, are not changing and have risen by 22 percent in three years.
expected: Arnsby University will cut rents on 1,300 rooms in its oldest halls by 15 percent, at a cost of 1.6 million euros a year, but rents in newer halls, up 22 percent in three years, will not change.

input: A two-year study in 40 secondary schools in the Ostermark region has tested whether banning mobile phones during the school day improves maths results. Half the schools introduced a full ban, while the other half kept their existing rules. Pupils in schools with the ban scored on average 2 points higher on a standard 100-point maths test, but the researchers say this difference is within the margin of error and could be due to chance. They did find a clearer effect on behaviour: reported incidents of online bullying during school hours fell by 31 percent in schools with the ban. The study was funded by the regional education department.
expected: In a two-year study of 40 Ostermark schools, a phone ban was linked to maths scores 2 points higher, a difference within the margin of error, while reported online bullying during school hours fell 31 percent.

input: A start-up in the town of Brisholm has developed a hearing aid that adjusts itself automatically to background noise in restaurants, train stations and other busy places. In a trial with 150 users, 72 percent said they could follow conversations more easily than with their previous device. The device costs about 900 euros per pair, roughly a third of the price of comparable models. The company, Clearloop, says it plans to begin selling the device next spring. Audiologists involved in the trial cautioned that it was funded by the company and that participants knew which device they were using, which may have affected their answers.
expected: Brisholm start-up Clearloop's 900-euro self-adjusting hearing aid helped 72 percent of 150 trial users follow conversations more easily, but audiologists note the trial was company-funded and unblinded; sales start next spring.

input: Rents in the city of Calvenport rose by an average of 9.4 percent over the past year, the fastest increase since records began in 2005, according to the city's housing office. A typical two-bedroom flat now costs 1,240 euros a month. The office says the main cause is a shortage of new homes: only 640 were completed last year, against a target of 2,000. Short-term holiday lets also took about 1,100 flats off the long-term market. The city council will vote next month on a proposal to limit holiday lets to 90 nights a year in the central districts, a plan opposed by the local tourism association.
expected: Calvenport rents rose a record 9.4 percent in a year, driven by too few new homes and by holiday lets, and the council votes next month on capping central holiday lets at 90 nights a year.

input: The rollout of high-speed fibre broadband in the rural county of Elsmere has become a source of dispute. The network operator, Fennlink, says it has now connected 78 percent of homes, ahead of its target of 75 percent for this year. County councillors, however, say the figure counts homes where a cable passes the property, not homes that can actually order a service. Their own survey of 900 households found that only 52 percent could sign up. Fennlink says the difference reflects homes waiting for a final connection and that it will finish these by next summer. The county has asked the national regulator to clarify how coverage should be measured.
expected: Fennlink says its Elsmere fibre rollout reaches 78 percent of homes, beating its target, but councillors' survey found only 52 percent can order service, and the county has asked the regulator to define coverage.

input: Dairy farmers in the Rosswell district have started using a feed additive made from seaweed that reduces methane emissions from their cows. In a trial across 14 farms and about 2,000 cows, methane output fell by an average of 22 percent, while milk yields were unchanged. The additive costs farmers around 25 cents per cow per day, and the regional government is paying half of this for the first two years. The farmers' union welcomed the support but warned that many smaller farms could not afford the full cost afterwards. Researchers are also checking whether the additive has any effect on the taste of milk and cheese.
expected: A seaweed feed additive cut methane from about 2,000 cows on 14 Rosswell farms by 22 percent without lowering milk yields; the government covers half the cost for two years, but small farms fear the expense afterwards.

input: The town of Lindqvist has completed a district heating network that uses waste heat from a nearby paper mill to warm 2,800 homes and 40 public buildings. Households connected to the network are expected to pay about 25 percent less for heating than with individual gas boilers. The project cost 19 million euros and took three years to build. Officials estimate it will cut the town's carbon emissions by around 11,000 tonnes a year. The main risk, critics say, is that the network depends on a single mill, and the town has installed backup electric boilers in case the mill reduces production or closes.
expected: Lindqvist's 19 million euro district heating network now warms 2,800 homes and 40 public buildings with paper-mill waste heat, which is expected to cut heating bills by about 25 percent, though critics warn it depends on a single mill.

input: Energy supplier Valecrest Power has agreed to refund 18,000 customers a total of 2.3 million euros after overcharging them for more than a year. The regional energy regulator found that the company had failed to apply a price cut to customers on older fixed-rate contracts. The average refund will be about 128 euros, paid automatically into customers' accounts by the end of next month. Valecrest has also been fined 400,000 euros. The company said the error was caused by a billing system upgrade and apologised. Consumer advocates welcomed the refunds but said customers should not have had to wait for the regulator to step in.
expected: Valecrest Power will refund 18,000 customers 2.3 million euros, about 128 euros each, and pay a 400,000 euro fine after the regulator found it failed to apply a price cut to older fixed-rate contracts.

input: Housing has been at the centre of debate in Wrenfield since the closure of the shipyard in 2015 left large areas of the waterfront empty. Several developers have proposed schemes over the years, but none has got past the planning stage, and residents have campaigned against high-rise towers. The planning committee on Wednesday approved a plan by developer Harbourline to build 520 homes on the former shipyard site, of which 30 percent will be affordable. The scheme includes a public park and buildings no taller than eight storeys. A day later, the council confirmed that the decision must be ratified by the full council because of a procedural error, and the vote is now expected in November.
expected: Wrenfield's planning committee approved Harbourline's plan for 520 homes, 30 percent affordable, on the former shipyard site, but a procedural error means the full council must ratify it in a vote expected in November.

input: A court in Haverton has ordered a waste disposal company to pay 650,000 euros in fines and clean-up costs after it illegally dumped construction waste on farmland over a period of three years. Investigators found around 9,000 tonnes of rubble, plastic and insulation material on two fields near the village of Marsh End. The company's director, Paul Grend, was also given a suspended prison sentence of 18 months. The judge said the company had acted purely for profit and saved itself an estimated 400,000 euros in landfill fees. The farmer who owns the land said the fields may not be usable for at least five years.
expected: A Haverton court ordered a waste firm to pay 650,000 euros in fines and clean-up costs and gave its director an 18-month suspended sentence for dumping about 9,000 tonnes of waste on farmland near Marsh End.

input: Bus drivers in the city of Torrance will strike for 48 hours next week after talks over pay broke down. The drivers' union says its members have been offered a 3 percent rise, while inflation over the past year was 5.8 percent. About 900 drivers are expected to walk out, which would halt most of the city's 62 bus routes. The bus company says it cannot afford more without cutting services or raising fares, and that drivers already earn more than in neighbouring cities. Both sides have agreed to meet with a mediator on Monday, and the union says the strike could be called off if a better offer is made.
expected: About 900 Torrance bus drivers plan a 48-hour strike next week, halting most of the city's 62 routes, after rejecting a 3 percent pay offer against 5.8 percent inflation; mediated talks on Monday could avert it.

input: Scientists at the Northgate University observatory have discovered a comet that will pass close enough to Earth next March to be seen with binoculars. The comet, named Hollis-Varga after the two students who first spotted it in survey images, is currently about 380 million kilometres away. Its closest approach to Earth will be about 70 million kilometres, which poses no risk. Astronomers estimate its nucleus is around 2 kilometres wide. They warned, however, that comets are hard to predict: it could brighten enough to be seen with the naked eye, or break apart as it nears the Sun, as about one in ten such comets do.
expected: Northgate University astronomers have found comet Hollis-Varga, which will pass a harmless 70 million kilometres from Earth next March and should be visible with binoculars, though it could brighten further or break up near the Sun.

input: Electricity prices in the Tarvik region have risen more slowly than in neighbouring areas over the past two years, a development that has been widely credited to the large solar parks built on former mining land. A report published this week by the regional energy agency challenges that view. It says the solar parks, which supply about 18 percent of the region's power, account for less than a third of the price difference. The main factor, according to the agency, was a long-term gas contract signed in 2021 that locked in prices well below the market. That contract expires next year, and the agency expects bills to rise by 10 to 15 percent.
expected: A Tarvik energy agency report says the region's slower electricity price rises owe more to a cheap 2021 gas contract than to solar parks, and expects bills to rise 10 to 15 percent when the contract expires next year.

input: The town of Brackenford will introduce a 20 km/h speed limit on 35 residential streets from next month, following a year-long trial on six streets near schools. During the trial, average speeds fell from 31 km/h to 24 km/h, and there were no injury collisions, compared with five in the previous year. New signs and road markings for the wider scheme will cost about 140,000 euros. The town will not install speed cameras but will rely on police checks and community speed watches. A local drivers' group said the limit was too low for some wider streets and has asked the council to reconsider eight of them.
expected: Brackenford will extend a 20 km/h limit to 35 residential streets after a trial cut average speeds from 31 to 24 km/h with no injury collisions, though a drivers' group wants eight wider streets reconsidered.

input: A court in Selmont ruled last year that the city's ban on overnight parking for camper vans breached national law, and around 70 people who had been living in vans near the harbour were allowed to stay. The city appealed. On Friday, the regional appeal court overturned the earlier ruling, finding that cities may restrict overnight parking for safety and sanitation reasons as long as they offer alternative sites. The city says it will open a designated site with 40 places, water and toilets by the end of the year. Campaigners argue that 40 places will not be enough and are considering a further appeal to the national court.
expected: An appeal court overturned a ruling against Selmont's overnight camper-van parking ban, allowing limits if alternative sites exist; the city plans a 40-place site, which campaigners say is too small and may challenge further.

input: A new walk-in mental health service for young people aged 16 to 25 has opened in the centre of Rydal, offering same-day appointments with counsellors without a referral from a doctor. The service is run by the charity Open Door and funded for three years by a 1.2 million euro grant from the regional health authority. In its first six weeks it saw 410 young people, more than twice the number expected. Staff say most visitors came for help with anxiety, stress at university or family problems. Because of the demand, waiting times on busy afternoons have already reached two hours, and the charity is recruiting four more counsellors.
expected: Rydal's new walk-in mental health service for 16 to 25-year-olds saw 410 people in six weeks, more than twice the expected number, pushing busy-afternoon waits to two hours; the charity is hiring four more counsellors.

input: The Ferndale city council and the local football club Ferndale United disagree sharply over the cost of a proposed new stadium. The club says the 15,000-seat ground on the edge of town would cost 45 million euros and bring in 6 million euros a year in extra spending at local businesses. An independent review commissioned by the council puts the cost at 62 million euros and finds that most of the extra spending would simply move from other parts of town. The club wants the council to provide the land and guarantee a loan of 20 million euros. Councillors will decide in January whether to support the project.
expected: Ferndale United says its 15,000-seat stadium would cost 45 million euros and boost local spending, but a council review puts the cost at 62 million with little net gain; councillors decide in January on land and a loan guarantee.

input: A tribunal in Kerrow has ruled that delivery company Swiftcart wrongly classified 230 of its couriers as self-employed and must treat them as workers entitled to holiday pay and the minimum wage. The couriers had argued that the company set their routes, controlled their working hours through its app and penalised them for refusing jobs. The tribunal agreed, saying the drivers had little real independence. Swiftcart estimates the ruling could cost it about 1.5 million euros in back pay. The company said it was disappointed and is considering an appeal, while the couriers' union said it would bring similar claims on behalf of another 600 drivers.
expected: A Kerrow tribunal ruled that Swiftcart wrongly treated 230 couriers as self-employed, entitling them to holiday pay and the minimum wage at an estimated 1.5 million euros in back pay; Swiftcart may appeal.

input: Nurses at St Aldric's Hospital in Pendlebury have voted to accept a new pay deal, ending a dispute that led to four one-day strikes this year. The agreement gives nurses a 6.5 percent rise over two years and adds a 1,000-euro bonus for those working regular night shifts. About 74 percent of union members who voted backed the deal, on a turnout of 61 percent. The hospital will also hire 45 extra nurses to reduce the use of agency staff, which cost it 3.2 million euros last year. Some nurses said the deal did not address workloads, and the union says it will monitor staffing levels closely.
expected: Nurses at St Aldric's Hospital accepted a 6.5 percent two-year pay rise plus a 1,000-euro night-shift bonus, ending a dispute that caused four strikes; 45 nurses will be hired, though workload concerns remain.

input: A team at the Corvan Agricultural Research Centre has found that planting wildflower strips along the edges of wheat fields reduced aphid damage without the need for extra pesticides. Over three seasons on 30 farms, fields with flower strips had 38 percent fewer aphids on average, because the flowers attracted ladybirds and parasitic wasps that feed on them. Wheat yields were about 4 percent higher. The strips take up roughly 3 percent of each field, which the researchers say is more than compensated for by the reduced pest damage. They caution that the effect was weaker in very dry years, when fewer flowers bloomed.
expected: A three-season study on 30 farms found wildflower strips along wheat fields cut aphids by 38 percent and raised yields about 4 percent by attracting predators, though the effect was weaker in very dry years.

input: The coastal town of Gullhaven has banned single-use plastic cups, cutlery and food containers at all events on public land, starting next summer. The rule will apply to the town's 25 annual festivals and markets, which council officials say generate about 14 tonnes of plastic waste each year. Organisers will need to use reusable or compostable items, and the council will provide a washing station for reusable cups at larger events. Event organisers who break the rule could face fines of up to 2,000 euros. Some small food vendors say compostable packaging costs up to three times as much, and have asked for a temporary subsidy.
expected: Gullhaven will ban single-use plastic cups, cutlery and containers at events on public land from next summer, targeting about 14 tonnes of waste a year, but small vendors say alternatives cost up to three times more.

input: Workers at the Brenna Glassworks in the town of Oldmere have agreed to a shorter week for six months to avoid redundancies, after the factory lost two major orders. Under the deal, about 340 employees will work 32 hours instead of 40 and receive 90 percent of their normal pay, with the difference partly covered by a regional short-time work scheme. The company had earlier warned that up to 80 jobs could be cut. Union representatives said the agreement was the best option available but warned that many workers would struggle with the lower income. Management will review the arrangement in March depending on new orders.
expected: About 340 Brenna Glassworks employees in Oldmere will work a 32-hour week at 90 percent pay for six months to avoid up to 80 job cuts, with a review in March depending on new orders.

input: The ferry service between Port Iver and the island of Skerra will run all year round from next January, instead of only between April and October. The regional transport authority has agreed to pay a subsidy of 1.8 million euros a year to cover the winter months, when passenger numbers are low. Island residents, of whom there are about 1,400, have had to rely on a small mail boat that runs twice a week during winter. The operator will use a smaller ship of 200 passengers on winter crossings. The service could be suspended if storms make the crossing unsafe, which happened on 19 days last winter for the mail boat.
expected: From January the Port Iver to Skerra ferry will run all year with a 1.8 million euro annual subsidy, giving about 1,400 islanders, who have relied on a twice-weekly mail boat in winter, a year-round service, though storms may still force suspensions.

input: A survey by the Harland Consumer Council has found that the cost of a typical weekly shopping basket varies by up to 19 percent between supermarkets in the same town. Researchers checked the prices of 40 everyday items, such as bread, milk, rice and washing-up liquid, in 120 stores across the region. Discount chains were cheapest on average, but the survey found that some branches of the same chain charged different prices depending on their location, with stores in wealthier neighbourhoods charging around 4 percent more. The council is calling for clearer unit pricing on shelves so shoppers can compare products more easily.
expected: A Harland Consumer Council survey of 40 items in 120 stores found weekly basket costs varied by up to 19 percent, with some chains charging about 4 percent more in wealthier areas; it wants clearer unit pricing.

input: A farm in the hills above Velmont has become the first in the region to grow rice commercially, using fields that are flooded by water from a small mountain stream. The farm harvested 18 tonnes this autumn from 4 hectares, about half the yield of farms in traditional rice-growing areas. The owners, Lena and Marco Duvel, say warmer summers over the past decade made the crop possible. They sell the rice directly to local restaurants and shops at around 6 euros a kilo. Agricultural experts say the project is interesting but warn that water rights may become a problem in dry summers, when the stream also supplies nearby villages.
expected: A farm above Velmont has become the region's first commercial rice grower, harvesting 18 tonnes from 4 hectares thanks to warmer summers, but experts warn water rights could become a problem in dry summers.

input: The last department store in the town of Corbridge Hill will close in February after 112 years, its owners announced on Friday. The four-storey Haldane and Rook store employs 64 people, all of whom will be offered redundancy pay or jobs at the company's two remaining branches. Sales at the store have fallen by around 40 percent over the past decade as shoppers moved online and to an out-of-town retail park. The owners said the building needed about 2 million euros of repairs that they could not justify. The town council hopes to turn the building into flats and smaller shops and has begun talks with the owners about buying it.
expected: Corbridge Hill's 112-year-old Haldane and Rook department store will close in February after a 40 percent fall in sales, affecting 64 staff, and the council is in talks to buy the building for flats and shops.

input: The public library in the town of Esterby has started lending musical instruments, from guitars and violins to keyboards and a small drum kit. The collection of 85 instruments was built from donations by residents and a 15,000-euro grant from the regional arts council. Library members can borrow an instrument for up to four weeks free of charge, and a local music school offers two free beginner lessons with each loan. Within a month, every instrument was on loan and more than 200 people were on the waiting list. Librarians say the biggest challenge is repairs: several instruments have already been returned with broken strings or damaged cases.
expected: Esterby library now lends 85 donated and grant-funded musical instruments free for up to four weeks; all were borrowed within a month and over 200 people are waiting, though repairs are becoming a problem.
